title: I Used to Say 'I Have a Bad Memory' but Now I Know It Was Just Untrained
author: Keiffenheim, Eva
summary: Eva Keiffenheim argues that 'I have a bad memory' is a misdiagnosis rooted in a misunderstanding of how memory works rather than an accurate self-assessment. Drawing on the 2017 Dresler et al. Neuron study (six weeks of method-of-loci training doubled word recall -- from 26 to 62 out of 72 -- and changed brain connectivity patterns in ways resembling memory athletes, with improvements persisting months later) and Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 retrieval practice study, she distinguishes between working memory (small, temporary, bottlenecked) and long-term memory (near-unlimited capacity, grows with learning). The fluency illusion -- mistaking recognition for recall because the source material is in front of you -- explains why re-reading, highlighting, and summarizing feel productive but produce poor retention: the page is doing the remembering, not the reader. The single highest-leverage move she recommends is switching from restudying to retrieval practice: closing the source, trying to recall, checking, then retrieving again -- because the effortful strain of almost-remembering is precisely how stronger memory traces are built. Memory champions are not born with exceptional brains; they have learned and practiced techniques like the memory palace, which use existing long-term memory patterns to compress new information into meaningful chunks, effectively expanding working memory capacity for related content.
points: Working memory and long-term memory are functionally distinct: 'bad memory' complaints almost always describe a working-memory bottleneck or an encoding/retrieval failure, not a storage problem -- long-term memory has near-unlimited capacity and grows with learning.

The fluency illusion is the core cognitive trap: re-reading and highlighting feel productive because the material is present, but the brain mistakes recognition (the page is remembering) for recall (you are remembering), and recognition does not build durable memory traces.

Retrieval practice consistently outperforms restudying at any delay beyond a few hours -- Roediger and Karpicke (2006) found dramatically superior retention after a week for students who practiced free recall rather than restudying, even when re-reading felt more effective in the short term.

Chunking works because long-term memory encodes patterns; 1492 is one chunk to someone who knows history, not four digits -- building domain knowledge in long-term memory effectively expands working memory capacity for new information in that domain.

The 2017 Dresler et al. study proved that memory training is genuine neurological restructuring, not trivial memorization tricks: six weeks of practice changed brain connectivity patterns in ways that predicted memory improvements months later.
quotes: For most of my life, I called this a personal flaw. I have a bad memory. I said it the way some people say I'm bad at math. I used it as half excuse, and half self-diagnosis, fully in the victim mode of I can't change anything about this.

In a 2017 study published in Neuron, researchers worked with a set of people who had no memory training, no special talent, and put them through six weeks of method-of-loci practice. Their word recall more than doubled, from an average of 26 words to 62 out of 72.

Working memory is the small, temporary workspace you use when information is new, unorganized, and not yet connected to anything you already know. It's why a random string like 8-3-1-9-4-0-2-6 vanishes the moment someone interrupts you.
The other part is long-term memory and it works very different from your short-term memory. Its capacity is close to unlimited and the more you learn the more you can remember.

Cognitive scientists call this trap the fluency illusion. The page is doing the remembering for you, and your brain mistakes recognition for recall. You read the line, and think you got it. But when you need the idea later -- for example at the dinner party -- the source isn't there and you wonder why you 'knew it yesterday' but you can't recall it today.

Roediger and Karpicke ran the most-cited version of this experiment. In their 2006 experiment, students studied prose passages and either restudied them or practiced free recall. When tested after a very short delay, restudying looked better. But after longer delays -- especially a week -- retrieval practice led to substantially better retention.

Stop re-reading. Start retrieving, for example, through a spaced repetition system. After you read something, close the source. Try to write down what you remember. Then check. Try to recall the argument. Then go back and look. The act of pulling -- straining, getting it half-right, finding the gap -- is how you build a stronger memory trace.
